newsitem.title: USA: Cannabis club reopens in San Francisco.
newsitem.headline: Cannabis club reopens in San Francisco.

text.p: Hundreds of people suffering from AIDS and other illnesses lined up to buy marijuana legally on Wednesday when a San Francisco club that supplies the drug to the sick reopened under a court order.
Within a few hours, the San Francisco Cannabis Cultivators' Club had given out about 700 applications for membership and 200 people had already bought marijuana, club founder Dennis Peron said.
"What a day! It's a great day. It feels like victory, like a turning point in our whole country's history," he said.
The club operated in defiance of the law, serving around 12,000 clients, until California Attorney General Dan Lungren won a court order closing it down last August.
At the time Lungren's office accused the club of routinely selling marijuana to children and to people with forged doctors' notes or with no medical justification.

But in November, California voters approved Proposition 215 which allows sick people and their "primary caregiver" to legally possess and grow marijuana for medical use when recommended by a doctor. Arizona voters passed a similar measure.
A San Francisco Superior Court judge ruled last week that the club could reopen provided it operated in accordance with that measure.

Peron said the club was calling applicants' doctors to check they recommended marijuana for them. Once approved, members go to the club's bar where they pay between $5 and $50 for one-eighth of an ounce (22 g) of marijuana, depending on grade. The club also sells marijuana in cookies and other items.

Peron said the first bag of marijuana was bought by a 27-year-old AIDS patient. Supporters of medical marijuana say the drug often eases nausea in cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy, help AIDS patients gain an appetite and lowers eye pressure in glaucoma sufferers.

Possession or sale of marijuana remains illegal under federal law, even for medicinal use. The Clinton administration, which opposed the California and Arizona measures, has vowed to sanction doctors who prescribe marijuana.

A spokeswoman for Sen. Dianne Feinstein, a California Democrat who opposed Proposition 215, said the senator would meet with officials of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to discuss whether a carefully drawn amendment to the federal Controlled Substances Act should be drafted to clarify the conflict between federal and state law caused by the passage of the California and Arizona measures.

If an amendment to the act was necessary and could be tightly drawn to allow medicinal use of marijuana "in very limited circumstances for terminally ill patients, that might be something (Feinstein) would consider," spokeswoman Susan Kennedy said.
"Any amendment would have to be very tightly drawn to permit use in an extremely limited number of circumstances with tight control. This may not be feasible," Kennedy said.
She stressed that Feinstein was opposed to legalising marijuana and that "any language that opened up the use of marijuana for illegitimate purposes...is going down the wrong road."
